name: Tatoosh Range Traverse
region: Tatoosh Range, Mount Rainier National Park

legs.connect: Follow the crest along from the Unicorn area; the rock on Boundary is steeper than the walking between peaks, with a low fifth class crack.
Continue along the crest past West Unicorn; Foss is no harder than a scramble.
Follow the ridge on; the summit rock is low fifth class and comes down by scrambling or a short rappel.
Descend Castle's far side and cross the saddle; the east arete is airy low fifth class, with a side trail for coming off.
Short walk on well-used paths from Pinnacle; often only passed.
Continue along the crest; the final approach uses a couloir.
Back down into the saddle and up a steep couloir of small gullies; climb one at a time to protect the party below.
Bushy, slow ground follows, then a short third-class scramble to the top.
Thick timber and bushwhacking make this the slowest stretch; the summit is often just passed on the ridge.
Final summit; an easy trail gives the way up and down, though a steep wall is possible for those wanting more.

how: Climbers usually start at the Snow Lake trailhead and go west, tagging Unicorn first and then working along the crest over Boundary, Foss, Castle, Pinnacle, Plummer, Denman, Lane, Wahpenayo, Chutla and Eagle. Several summits are low fifth class rock; most others are scrambles. Stevens, at the far east end, is usually left out of the one-day version because it adds a long detour. Bring a helmet and a short rope if you plan to rappel Unicorn and Castle.
descent: Most parties finish down the easy Eagle Peak trail to the road, then either use a shuttle car at Longmire or walk the road back to the starting trailhead.
logistics: Park entry fee applies. A car at each end saves the road walk. Best in summer when the snow chute under Unicorn has thinned but is still there to climb; fill water at the lake early because the crest is dry.
notes: One report skipped Stevens, did Boundary before West Unicorn and mentions no rappels; the FKT run included Stevens and rappelled Unicorn and Castle with a 30 m rope. Order of Boundary/Stevens/Foss varies. Mountaineers route page returned 403, not read. Plummer and Chutla often only passed.

name: Unicorn, Boundary and Stevens Peaks
region: Tatoosh Range, Mount Rainier National Park

legs.connect: Go along the crest from the Unicorn area; the rock on Boundary is a low fifth class crack.
Optional third summit at the far east end of the range; it needs a long detour and an early start.

how: From Snow Lake, climb the snow chute and notch to Unicorn's summit block, then pair it with the seldom-climbed Boundary Peak next door. Stevens is a longer addition at the east end of the range that turns the outing into a very long day. Carry helmet, axe and crampons in early season, plus a few small cams for the rock.
descent: Retrace the route to Snow Lake; glissade the upper slopes and chute when the snow allows. Boundary has a side trail on its west side.
logistics: One car-to-car day from the Snow Lake trailhead; park entry fee applies. Start very early if adding Stevens.
notes: Mazamas page does not give the order of the three peaks; the Mountaineers page for this trio returned 403 so was not read.

name: Mount Howard to Aneroid Mountain Ridge

legs.connect: Follow a trail south along the ridge; a lower bypass trail skips this summit and saves about 400 feet of gain.
Drop to a saddle with a large boulder and climb its southwest ridge; the trail braids and fades near the crest.
Descend to the next saddle and climb about 560 feet of loose ground with no clear path.

how: Ride the tram up, walk to Mount Howard, then follow the high ridge south over East Peak and Hidden Peak to Aneroid, the highest of the group. It is hiking and loose scrambling with no technical climbing, but steep and strenuous. East Peak and Hidden Peak can each be skipped by a bypass path. Allow five to six hours out and back.
descent: Either return along the ridge to the last tram, or go down Aneroid's loose southwest ridge to Dollar Pass and walk out the East Fork trail to the lake.
logistics: The tram runs from late May to September and the last ride down is mid-afternoon, so take an early one if returning that way. No water is available along the ridge until near Dollar Pass.
notes: 2017 and 2021 trip reports are by one author; 2019 report and the guide page are independent. A Pete's Point extension from Dollar Pass/Jewett Lake was reached in 2021 and turned back by wind in 2019; not entered as its own link-up.
